title: Standards — consumption tracker
subject: main
summary: Temporary: which auto-generated rules were digested into canonical docs.

standards.note: Every rule from `_meta/_docs_to_consume/standards/`, verbatim, with consumption status. A rule is consumed when it lands in a consumer doc. IDs are append-only: never renumber, never reuse a retired number.

files.governs: folder structure & placement — universal (API, frontend, mobile)

rules.text: Layer folders everywhere: `middlewares/ routes/ services/ repositories/ models/` — identical at every level (seed slice, product slice, app). Always folders, even for one file; scaffolding never changes shape.
One abstraction per file, maximally separated.
Models: `<entity>.model.ts` + `<entity>.schemas.ts` side by side, in a folder named `models` (never `schemas`).

One canonical **model** per entity, one declarer — re-declaring elsewhere is a violation. Models carry no business logic. *(open: Daniel — "sometimes some logic in the model"; exact wording unresolved.)*
Zod schemas are inferred from the Drizzle model (drizzle-zod), never hand-written; types for dynamic data infer from the Zod schema.
An entity's schema lives in its slice's shared folder and is consumed by all apps of that slice. A slice = a seed slice or the app (never a product slice).
rules.note: Destined for `backend-composition` — that doc's axiom 1 already owns entity/schema ownership. Un-consumed from `scaffolding-and-import-boundaries` on 2026-08-11: scaffolding owns placement and import boundaries, not what lives inside the layers. CORRECTION on digestion: the second sentence is wrong — a slice is a seed slice or an product slice, never `the app`. See the glossary and scaffolding axiom 1.

rules.text: Module entities in `<seed slice>/api/models/`; product slice entities in `apps/main/slices/product/<f>/api/models/` — same shape, one declarer each; `src/models/index.ts` re-exports only (db-client aggregation), declares nothing.
rules.note: Text updated 2026-07-24: product slices are full-stack slices under `apps/main/slices/product/<f>/` (api / web + shared), same anatomy as seed slices. Was: app entities in `product slices/<f>/models/`. Destined for `backend-composition` — that doc's axiom 1 already owns entity/schema ownership. Un-consumed from `scaffolding-and-import-boundaries` on 2026-08-11: scaffolding owns placement and import boundaries, not what lives inside the layers. CORRECTION on digestion: this rule's paths are the right ones. The `backend-composition` draft is stale — it still says app-specific entities live in `apps/main/shared/api/src/models/`, predating the product slices restructure.

rules.text: Shared code lives in a folder named `shared`, at the nearest level to its consumers — api-internal helpers in `api/shared/` (replaces `api/lib/`); api↔web code in the seed slice's top-level `shared/`. No `lib` folders for shared code.
Helpers are self-sufficient: no DB access, data passed in.
Once-only init (server, db pool, redis) lives at `src/` root, never in a lib/shared folder.

Placement ladder (first fit wins): pure data → `configs/` · generic engine → `shared/libs/` · reusable slice → `apps/main/slices/seed/` · this-app product logic → `product slices/` · wiring → app shell.
A configs folder never has its own libs subfolder.
rules.note: Parked for the config-architecture doc; decided while building 02.

rules.text: Integration code for a **consumed** provider lives in its own folder, not `api/` — `api/` is what you expose, not what you consume.
The seed baseline contains zero DB migrations — migrations belong to products built from the seed.
rules.note: Parked — belongs to a db/baseline doc (likely 03), not scaffolding; decided while building 02.

rules.text: README is a pointer to the docs, not the docs.
rules.note: Parked for the documentation doc (DOC rules); decided while building 02.

rules.text: `apps/main/shared/api` has no product logic. It mounts seed slices, wires them together, injects what they need. Its only app-level logic is cross-seed slice hook plumbing, centralized in one place.
The app imports only seed slice public surfaces (`api/index.ts` barrels). No deep imports into seed slice internals — anywhere.

Seed slices never import each other. Cross-seed slice connections live only in the app's hooks wiring in api/src/mounts.ts : seed slices emit fact-only lifecycle hooks; the app decides and may call another seed slice's public service.
A hook carries the bare fact only — message/template content is exported separately.
A seed slice that receives an external webhook owns it exclusively and translates it into an internal lifecycle hook; other seed slices react to the hook, never the webhook.
Seed slices never import configs, db, or loggers — they declare needs; the app injects at mount.
rules.note: Consumed by scaffolding axiom 3 (`a slice imports only libs and packages... injected by the app`), which states it more completely — it also names leaf adapters. No separate reference claim.

rules.text: Seed slices import only node modules or internal shared libraries. Libraries import only node modules — never other libraries. Seed slices and libraries carry zero product knowledge.
Library ≠ seed slice: library = low-level reusable engine + adapters, zero product knowledge; seed slice = configurable, product-facing slice reusable across apps.
rules.note: Absorbed by the glossary: the terms library and seed slice carry these definitions. A claim that defines terms is the glossary´s job.

rules.text: Seed slices are self-contained and reusable across projects. App product slices are product-specific, need not be self-contained, and may import each other (a product slice is a code-org convention, not an import boundary). Same internal scaffolding either way.
rules.note: Consumed by scaffolding axiom 4 (`slices differ in one thing only: whether they may reach each other`). No separate reference claim.

rules.text: The app owns all routing and mounts every route a seed slice exports.
Removal test: deleting a seed slice = delete its folder + mount line(s) + hook line(s) + configs. Nothing else breaks. One touch point (the mount) between seed slice and app.
rules.note: Absorbed by scaffolding´s Purpose (decoupability states the removal test near-verbatim). No separate reference claim.

rules.text: Client-facing and machine-to-machine (M2M) routes are distinct top-level paths.

files.governs: routes → services → repositories → models; naming; errors/logs

rules.text: Five layers, one responsibility each: middleware (hydration/auth) → router (HTTP transport) → service (business logic) → repository (data access) → model.
Only repositories touch the database — read and write, no exception. Two valid paths: middleware→router→service→repo→db, or middleware→repo→db (hydration reads only).
Backends with no API surface (e.g. cron over self-contained libraries) are exempt from the 5-layer/2-path rule.
One repository = one table.

Standard method set per repo: `findAll` (paginated: identical WHERE for list + count, returns `{ rows, total }`), `findByIds` (always an array — want one? pass `[id]`; no `findById`), `create`, `update`, `delete`. Full CRUD present even if currently unused.

Extra repo methods only for a genuinely specific query shape, with a stated reason. Named for the field filtered, plural, array params: `findAllByOrgIds`, never `listFor*`. Specificity and product constraints are the role of services, not repos.

Repos are dumb: zero business logic — no conditional, switch, throw, or decision. A repo never throws; it returns empty state. A permission-style lookup returns rows/count, never a boolean (boolean = business logic).

No hand-written joins in a repo. AC-built queries may contain joins — for permission scoping and for display/enrichment alike (see AC7). Any other cross-entity read: service enrichment or a DB view — case-by-case call.
Views end in `View`. A view lives in the repository of its base entity and is that repo's queryable relation.
Every model/table gets a repository and a service — the service may be a thin route→repo proxy.
Services hold the logic. They never touch db or SQL.

In a seed slice, a service calls only its own entity's repository; it reaches other entities through **their service** — never their repo. Cross-entity access is always service-to-service. (App product slices may be looser: product slices can reach each other.)
rules.note: Absorbed by backend-composition axioms (the five layers and the fixed call graph). No separate reference claim.

rules.text: A service calling another service as a pure pass-through (no added logic) is removed — call the underlying service directly.
rules.note: Removed from the backend-composition draft on Daniel's review (2026-08-11) — claim wording vague and imprecise. Restate precisely before digesting, or drop.

rules.text: Entity-creation logic centralizes in the owning service, never duplicated inline by callers.
rules.note: Removed from the backend-composition draft on Daniel's review (2026-08-11) — claim wording vague and imprecise. Restate precisely before digesting, or drop.

rules.text: Every service method has a real consumer — unused service methods are deleted (repos are the exception: API5).
rules.note: Removed from the backend-composition draft on Daniel's review (2026-08-11) — claim wording vague and imprecise. Restate precisely before digesting, or drop.

rules.text: Meaningful slice actions get their own named service method (`publish`, `accept`), never an overloaded `update`.
rules.note: Removed from the backend-composition draft on Daniel's review (2026-08-11) — claim wording vague and imprecise. Restate precisely before digesting, or drop.

rules.text: Services throw typed `AppError` subclasses only (`lib/error.ts`), never raw `new Error()`. The service is the only layer that throws.
Routers are thin: extract request identity, zod-parse input, call one service, return. Never import a repo or db; zero business logic; never decide access.
Design and finalize routes first — the route is the interface; the service shape emerges from routes + repo.

Middleware hydrates blindly — no business branching (no if/else on session validity; the service throws when there's no session). Hydration is the one sanctioned exception to "all DB access goes through AC": it must read the DB *before* AC exists (it produces the bag AC needs), so it uses a dedicated method minted by scoped AC that reaches the DB without a Scope. Kept safe by being a public service method with no route exposing it.
Protected requests pass a fixed linear middleware sequence before the handler: set/validate session → fetch roles/memberships → hydrate effective-permissions bag → unmet-requirements gate (see GATE).
Global error handler wired once, in `server.ts`. Every error body includes `requestId`. No internal details in responses.
pino only, no `console.*`. Shape: `logger.warn({ err, ...ctx }, "msg")` — object first, Error on `err`. No PII in logs beyond ids.
Repos use `find*`; services use `get*`; `load*` is reserved for config — and a config loader is never named like a DB accessor. Layers don't share one name: repo `findByX` → service `getByX`.
`getMy*` is allowed in services.
Multi-record lookups are plural and take array params; singular names only for single-unique-entity lookups.
Mutate endpoints are named `update`, not `patch`.
Recovery/reset endpoints are named after the slice object (`completePasswordRecovery`), not generic verbs.
Public endpoint names never leak internal mechanism (`register`, not `flows`); services are named for what they do, not how (`auth`, not `relay`).
`getCurrent*` is `getLatest*` when no rollback exists — names reflect what the system actually does.

`me` namespace = data of the requesting user and no organization. A route is `me` only if both hold: it touches no other user's data, and it works without an active org. Fails the first → `admin` (ban/suspend/delete) or the entity's route; fails the second → the entity's route under the active org. `me` routes are exactly the ones allowed to run with no active-org context.
Route grouping follows the primary entity retrieved, not URL nesting (`/organization/invitations` is an invitation route); a route path need not match its service name.
Identity-provider-specific lookups never live in the generic user model/service — they belong to the integration layer.
Immutable classification fields (e.g. org type) never change post-creation; denormalize them onto dependent records for convenience.
Request-scoped, client-owned state (e.g. active org) is never persisted — the client sends it every request; the server re-derives and re-checks. (Exception: real-time server-initiated actions.)

files.governs: ALL access control: engine, DSL, library isolation, public/private typing

rules.text: Default deny: protected endpoints grant zero access; only an explicit rule grants any.
The database is private-first: public rows/fields are the narrow, explicit exception — never the default, and never a public-permission join added to every query.
Every private/authenticated endpoint passes through the AC gate; public endpoints skip it.
The AC engine only returns query params (where/select/join) — it decides nothing, has no conditionals, is never a "god method".
Reads: the service is a pass-through; the resolver builds the WHERE/select/join, the repository executes it.
Create/update/delete: the service is the gate (allow/deny) before the write; repos and providers never decide.

All joins come from the AC resolver/DSL — permission-scoping joins and display/enrichment joins alike. Never hand-written in app code; the repo only executes them. Field-level access applies to join output (unpermitted fields come back blanked, not blocked).
rules.warning: Contradicted twice, so it stays un-consumed. The `repositories-never-join` decision (2026-08-12) already forbids any join in a repository, engine-built or not, which kills the display/enrichment half. And the engine narrows unpermitted columns out of the projection rather than blanking them — a restricted field list changes the SELECT, it never returns a nulled column. Needs a ruling on both halves before it can land.

rules.text: When AC evaluates a view, its config declares which entities compose that view — per-field access on join output resolves from the composing entities.
rules.warning: Not built. A view is an ordinary entity in the injected tables map: no config declares composing entities, and field access on it comes from the permission's own field list exactly as on a table. The access-control doc claims the built behaviour instead. Either this rule is aspirational or the library is under-built — unresolved.

rules.text: Create checks permission on the parent container (the entity doesn't exist yet); update/delete gate via a read-style query against the target — zero rows = denied.
rules.note: Both halves now hold, by a different route than this rule imagined. Update/delete gate via the read-style query. Create still computes no target — the row does not exist — but the `payload` slot added in roadmap step 4 gates it on the parent the new row points at, checked before the write. Not "permission on the parent container" as a container concept; a condition that follows the written row's own reference.

rules.text: Update/delete: cheap in-memory field-level check first, only then the row-level query.
rules.note: Built for update (`allowUpdate`). Delete has no field-level check — there are no columns to write — so the rule reads as update-only in the doc.

rules.text: A boolean gate is named `allow*`; a query-builder is named `resolve*`. Never one name for both.
Consumers may only narrow a resolved query (AND). OR at the root is forbidden (only nested inside an AND); no manually added OR clauses.
A per-method AC config may only restrict the base grant, never expand it.
rules.note: No per-method AC config exists yet; consumed as the general narrow-only rule alongside AC12.

rules.text: Access context (session, active org, effective permissions) is hydrated once in middleware and passed through all layers — never recomputed per layer.
Membership/roles re-resolve server-side every request against the active org; never trust a client-asserted role or org context.
Effective permissions resolve only from the active org's memberships. Exception: account-level security gates (2FA) evaluate across ALL memberships (see GATE5).
rules.note: The exception is stated here but owned by `unmet-requirements` (GATE5) — the two mechanisms are separate code paths.

rules.text: The router only classifies an endpoint public/private and passes through — it never gates, and it is not the public/private decision point. Visibility propagates conservatively: every method carries a typed public/private parameter, and private wins over public (public loses to private). AC lives between endpoint and repo, enforced not by a linter but by the branded DB-access methods and type design — reaching the DB without a Scope is a compile error.
rules.note: Split across two topics: the branded-scope half sits with the engine/gate, the visibility half with public/private typing.

rules.text: Every DB query is a branded/typed object only the gated AC lib can produce — no query can bypass AC.
rules.note: True of every query the gate runs. Two paths sit outside it by design and are documented as such: the named hydration handle, and reads a service runs after a gated lookup already admitted the caller.

rules.text: Requests with no active-org context resolve only user-level roles; membership-scoped checks are rejected, not passed through.
rules.note: "Rejected" is realised as a denial, not an error: the membership rule fails its context check, the scope compiles to FALSE, and the operation returns nothing.

rules.text: Context (session/env: role, org type) is checked in-memory before any query; context never triggers a DB query. Target = the specific entity acted on.
Keep the redundant context check even when the target check subsumes it — free defense-in-depth.
An endpoint invoked before any session exists must be public, not session-gated.
The DSL is explicit: no inference, no magic; flatten and name each part.
A permission = entity + action (+ optional access rule). No rule = unrestricted for matching entities; a rule only narrows.
Unset `fields` = all fields; a set list restricts read/update to those fields. Fields never default to deny.
Permissions are always leaves; roles are always branches — never nest a permission in a permission.
The role/permission hierarchy is a forest: one independent tree per org archetype.
rules.note: The doc says "org type", which is what the engine and config call it at runtime (`forests[orgType]`, `orgTypePath`). "Archetype" survives only in config comments — one of the two spellings should go.

rules.text: User roles and membership roles are separate DSLs; never cross-assignable.
rules.warning: Stated in the doc but NOT enforced. The account baseline and the org-type forests are one namespace with one global uniqueness check, and hydration unions baseline roles with membership roles into a single flat list — nothing would reject a baseline role granted on a membership. The separation is a convention today.

rules.text: Every permission/role has a unique name system-wide, even across archetypes (uniqueness enforced in the DSL layer as a redundant check).
Permission names: verb+entity, archetype qualifier when scoped; rules read as close to the path as possible.
Between permissions is OR; between rules inside one permission is AND.
rules.warning: Transcribed backwards, and the doc states the corrected rule. The engine ORs the rules inside a permission and ANDs the conditions inside one rule. The config already depends on the OR: `accept_own_invitation` carries two rules so an invitation matches by email OR by phone — read as AND it would require both, and no invitation carries both.

rules.text: Rules reference field names/values only, never storage shape — model changes never require rule changes.
Create-action rules declare no target (type-enforced); a target is never computed for create.

DSL symbols are distinct: `$` subject path, bare string entity path, quotes for literals; "lookup" (body-based: create/delete) is separate from "join" (relation-based: read/update). There is exactly ONE comparison operator, `has` (contains), which subsumes equality — contains covers string equality and membership in a vector alike; there is no separate equal/not-equal. `has not` (`..` / `!..`) exists in the notation but is currently unused.
rules.note: Consumed for the symbols. The single-operator rule was REPLACED in roadmap step 4, not kept: `has`/`hasNot` mean containment — and equality on a single-valued column, so a column becoming a list never touches a rule — while `is`/`isNot` are the strict single-value form and refuse a collection at boot. Splitting them is what makes containment safe: one operator meaning both would have made `invitation.email has $session.user.email` match by substring, letting a caller registered as "m@altar.io" accept an invitation addressed to "tim@altar.io". `lookup` never existed and is superseded by the `payload` slot; `has not` is now `hasNot` and is built, null-inclusive.

rules.text: No speculative DSL product slices — add when a real case needs them; rare edges handled in code.

Where a gate belongs, write `// gate: <action> on <entity> by <who>` — nothing else, no AC code. Methods that will need gating take `accessContext` as first parameter now. Pre-AC tenancy/validation methods stay, commented as placeholders, deleted when AC lands.
rules.note: Retired, not consumed: scoped AC has landed and is enforced in UOM, so the placeholder markers this rule governs no longer exist. Nothing to digest.

rules.text: The AC library knows nothing about the app, membership, org, or auth provider — it resolves roles→permissions from config only; runtime slice concepts arrive via a generic `bag` at call time.
Stack-agnostic: ORM and schema validator (Drizzle, Zod) are adapters; the query builds into where/join/select and only the repo executes it.
rules.warning: Half-built, and the doc claims only the built half. Zod sits behind a real port (`validate.ts` declares it, `adapters/zod.ts` implements it), but the ORM is not adapted: the engine and the gate import drizzle directly and emit drizzle SQL fragments. Swapping ORMs today means rewriting both. Either the rule overreaches or the port is missing.

rules.text: The AC library does no auth/session verification — it trusts the consumer's middleware.
The requester's roles stay separate from target-entity resolution — roles may come from a different source later.

Request-scoped cross-cutting data (subject, roles, permissions) travels in a generic `bag`, not anything named `session`. Services get only the minimal id they need unless they must resolve scope. Never build a service just to expose role/membership lookups — inject them into the bag.
rules.note: The container is generic, but every subject path the config writes is spelled `$session.*` and the bag type names a `session` key — the rule's own "not anything named session" is honoured by the library and dropped by the consumer.

rules.text: Every layer (route, service, repo) declares and types its own public/private flag; a cross-layer mismatch is a compile-time error. Public at the router = public all the way down. Repo/service private by default — explicit to expose.
Two authorization layers always: gate the caller id before the service AND re-pass and re-check at the repo — a repo is never trusted safe merely because its caller gates.

Architecture + AC conventions are enforced by linter rules wired into CI, consuming the documentation (enforce documented decisions, not the code). Pre-commit blocks on errors, warns on warnings. Rules apply uniformly — no rule-level carve-outs (special cases are business facts, not architecture exceptions).
rules.note: No destination doc yet. This governs how every doc is enforced, so it belongs with the DOC/PRC rules, which have no target document in the mind map. Un-consumed from `scaffolding-and-import-boundaries` on 2026-08-11.

files.governs: the unmet-requirements gate (428) — distinct from scoped AC

rules.text: The gate evaluates the caller's obligations (verified identifier, session factor, required profile data, legal consent) and returns clear / unmet. It never resolves queries.
Requirements classify as persistent (facts an account carries — e.g. verified email) or session-based (e.g. re-verify OTP this session).
Unmet requirements resolve one at a time, in fixed order; the response is HTTP **428** carrying the single next requirement.
The gate runs **before** scoped AC: an unmet requirement short-circuits with 428 before any AC-governed query executes.
Account-level security requirements (e.g. 2FA) evaluate across **all** memberships, not just the active org — switching org can't bypass them.
Frontend contract: on a 428, redirect automatically to the unmet-requirements resolution page — never leave the user stuck on the failed action.
Configs are pure, declarative data: no functions, no env reads, no runtime imports, no logic/methods/branching. Assembly happens in the app.
Env vars drive what mounts: which slices mount and which configs inject come from env vars, never hardcode. The pointer to which config is consumed lives outside the config object.
Config is authored as typed TypeScript source, not raw JSON — non-compliant config fails the build. Derive JSON later for external consumers if needed.
Config schemas reject contradictory combinations (e.g. `consent:true` with `shown:false`) — valid-combination rules, not free-form flags. Every config value has one identified consumer/owner.
Org/account policy (join mode, required consents, required auth factors, doc types) is declarative DSL, never implicit business logic. A new archetype + its rules = zero code, only config.

Never hardcode what the DSL is meant to make configurable — if it isn't consumed dynamically, the DSL is lying. Requirements over a model's fields derive dynamically from that model's schema (new fields auto-supported).
Archetype definitions centralize in one config file, never inferred ad hoc.

Every touch-point with an external provider routes through ONE abstraction/integration layer in its owning seed slice. App code never calls provider endpoints or imports the provider directly — the app must not even know the provider's name.
Provider data normalizes to the app's own shape at the boundary; slice vocabulary internally, never the provider's terms.

The auth provider owns authentication/identity only; orgs, memberships, roles, invitations are owned and implemented by the app. The provider must be self-hostable and cloud/surface-agnostic for core auth.

On user creation, a provider hook replicates the user into the app DB keyed by the provider's id; the app DB is the source of truth for its own records. Provider DB stays separate from the app DB. Provider fields (email, email-verified) are never persisted on the local user.

The backend proxies all identity-provider calls; the frontend never calls the provider or owns the session cookie (edge protection applies). Never issue auth-granting email/SMS links that auto-log-in — always explicit code entry.
Security-relevant inputs the provider doesn't validate (e.g. password policy from the DSL) validate locally — backend and frontend — before forwarding.

Registration splits into single-purpose services (submit identifier, submit credentials, verify); the verify call carries all remaining data (password, name, consents) in one request — no partial accounts.
Never two parallel sessions (in-house + provider) — one session is the source of truth.
No caching of provider or derived data by default — cache only when proven necessary.
All AC-DSL consumers are limited to the integration layer plus the login/register pages.
Confidence ranking: e2e UI > e2e HTTP-request > unit.

Before refactoring legacy code, write e2e HTTP tests to lock current behavior. Get all tests green (hack the impl if needed) before refactoring so the suite is trustworthy; keep them green through cleanup.
AC tests assert unhappy paths (unauthorized denied), not only happy paths.

Tests mount the app against their own configs, independent of dev/prod, so seed slice combinations test in isolation. Exhaustive edge-case config permutations live in the test config, not the seed baseline.
Migrating a suite: disable unsupported steps at the shared index — don't comment out or delete whole test files (keep intended coverage visible).

Markup carries only design-system attributes (`element=card`, state) and layout classes (flex/grid) — never raw appearance (padding, border, background), utility spacing/color classes, or inline styles. Appearance comes from one theme CSS keyed off attributes. Use the UI library's components and layout patterns.

Seed slices never assemble navigation (sidebars, menus) — they expose contracts (hooks, components); the host app assembles and mounts. Static/shared UI components live in shared libs; only the app instantiates and injects.
rules.note: Wording wrong, corrected on digestion into scaffolding-and-import-boundaries: a slice DOES assemble navigation over its own pages. The rule is ownership at the most specific level covering all targets — only cross-slice navigation belongs to the app.

rules.text: Frontend state stays minimal by default — no speculative global state architecture. Sensitive registration data (password, name, consents) lives in frontend state and ships in one request on verification success.

The frontend never enforces security — it hides/disables actions the user can't take and gives feedback; it never hard-blocks routes. Only allowed redirect: unauthenticated → login. Restricted pages render empty, not redirect.
Every config-driven role constraint has two consumers: frontend for UX, backend service for security. The frontend check is never sufficient.
rules.note: Digested by access-control rather than frontend-composition: the axiom "the frontend reflects, never decides" is access control's, and frontend-composition owns layout and composition, not authorization posture.

rules.text: Exactly three doc types: Map (navigation only — pointers, no rules/logic), Doc (canonical: Axiom → Purpose → Reference, in that order), ADR (append-only Context/Decision/Consequences + date, never inside canonical docs).

One index per level pointing only to other indexes/maps — no single global index. Each seed slice/library has its own docs folder starting with a map; a central map is referenced from the repo README.
A Map points only downstream (own slice + nested maps) — never upstream, never into another slice's files.
Docs are positional: a doc lives at the level it governs and applies to everything below. Each concept documented in exactly one place, never duplicated.
Axiom = short, inviolable, single idea per line, most-abstract-first; no subjectivity, no method names/shapes (those go in Reference). Reference is terse/diagrammatic. Minimum info per place.
Reusable-slice docs split "For Consumer" (how to use) from "For Contributor" (how to change).
Doc files number by reading order (01, 02…). Update order: draft axiom/reference + human approval → resolve reference gaps + approval → update reference → update index/navigation LAST.
Record an ADR journal entry before writing the canonical doc for an architecture change. No one edits a slice's code without first reading its architecture doc.
Verbally-agreed rules get written into canonical docs — never left in memory.
No doc/test is better than a wrong or half-right one; unreviewed docs move to a meta/review area before a refactor.
Documentation carries the principles, not every small decision — separate canonical rules from product slice descriptions/requirements; keep signal-to-noise high, less is more.

files.governs: design approaches, ways of working, agent rules

rules.text: Define the target architecture first, independent of current code; reviewing code destroys it. Agree schema/spec before coding — review architecture, not code. (Domain/ERD-first thinking lives here as an approach, not an enforced rule.)

Before writing a product slice, enumerate the exact files and each file's single responsibility; code only once fixed. Per-product slice architecture is required beyond general principles. Minimum files, simplest design.
Keep it simple by default; add complexity only when a concrete need appears. No abstractions for hypothetical needs — unnecessary/wrong abstractions are worse than dead code.

Lock a library/seed slice's public interface before building internals; rebuild from desired interfaces outward. When rewriting legacy, empty it out and reintroduce files one at a time — don't trim in place. New arch work happens in the real repo, not a parallel pilot.
Before writing an abstraction, pick and document a few canonical "perfect" reference implementations.

Extract a private helper only when reused in 2+ services; otherwise it stays a private method of its service. A pure function used by many services goes to the nearest shared folder (SCF8). Prefer functional code over classes.
Unconsumed = deleted. No speculative code, no "for later" scaffolding. (Repos' standard CRUD is the one exception — API5.)

Agents never read old code — not `_archive/`, not legacy code still in the repo. Everything needed is in: the step spec, the standards files the task assembles, and the files the spec names. If the spec doesn't say what something does — ask, don't dig.
Never let agents auto-apply edits; review each change as a PR diff, in small steps. Never delegate core entity/type design or large cleanup to agents unsupervised — small fixed-shape units, by hand.

Rules-driven codegen: architect writes the spec; implementer confirms agreement before building one unit at a time; auditor checks the diff against rules + spec. Disagree with a documented decision → raise it before diverging, never silently.
Don't hand the architecture linter's raw output to coding agents — the developer triages it (else agents route around rules).

Decide independently how you'd build it before reading existing code (avoid anchoring). Touch it, clean it. Keep an index of human-supervised vs AI-generated files; archive unverified code instead of deleting.
Logic changes and mechanical/naming changes land in separate commits — reviewers see the logic diff alone.

files.governs: UOM product slice design — product decisions, not architecture rules

rules.text: The UOM models: Organization · Membership (renamed from Member — it's a relationship, not a person) · Invitation · User · UserProfile · UserContacts · UserSystemPreferences · LegalDocument · ConsentRecord · OrganizationContacts. No OrganizationProfile in v1 — name, slug, logo/avatar, metadata live on Organization directly.
A user exists independent of their authentication identifiers; email/phone/OAuth are interchangeable identifiers, never the unique id.

All identifiers are unique — never the same email/phone twice, regardless of verification status. Unverified users can exist; verification no longer creates the user. *(Biggest logic refactor of the rebuild — lands in its own commit, separate from renames.)*
Public profile is a separate minimal entity (name, avatar) from the internal user; sensitive/optional data (contacts, preferences) live in separate tables from the core entity.
UserContacts exists so lists/joins can show email/phone — identifiers themselves live in the provider's DB, not ours.

OrganizationContacts is a link table `{ orgId, membershipId, contactId }`: a user owns many contacts; an org selects which of its members' contacts it holds. Repo + service, minimal. *(Table shape — dedicated vs pure link, one org per contact vs array — confirm with Daniel.)*
UserSystemPreferences: own model + repo + thin service (a route→repo proxy is fine). Not built yet.

Suspend is a **membership** state: the user can log in but has no access to that organization. Ban is a **user** state: no login — enforced post-login as a gate; the banned entity is the user, never identifiers. Delete is a **user** soft-delete: no login, identifiers become reusable by a new user. One dedicated service per transition. PII/GDPR anonymization: deferred until a product needs it.
Organization ownership is defined by the user's membership, never on the organization record.
One user cannot have more than one membership in one organization.

Persist only role names on the membership (with hierarchy context); granular permissions resolve at request time from config — role hierarchy and permissions live in config, not the database. Cascading is computed at runtime, always.
Active org is client-owned request state (header), never persisted server-side (API35).
UOM's only architectural distinction from any other slice is the hydration middleware. Everything else defers to access control.

`enrichedMembershipView` = membership ⋈ user ⋈ userProfile ⋈ userContacts, scoped by orgId; lives in the membership repository (API9). Serves the org members list and (with reduced columns) single-membership lookups.
LegalDocument and ConsentRecord are separate entities — separate models, repos, services — each with its own AC (documents gate who authors/publishes; consent gates who reads consent records).
Legal documents have no rollback: the lookup is `getLatestVersion`, not `getCurrent` (API30).
Privileged/system org types are never creatable via direct API calls — org type validates at the service layer, not just UI.
